questions.text:
Consider the relational database with the following four schemas and their respective instances.


The number of rows returned by the above SQL query is ___
questions.solution:
The query returns students for whom (D01 courses) EXCEPT (courses they registered) is empty, i.e. students registered for all D01 courses.

D01 courses = {C11, C12}.
- S01: C11, C12 True
- S02: C11 only False
- S03: C21, C22, C23 False
- S04: C11, C12 True
- S05: C11, C21 False

Answer: 2

questions.text:
Let [latex]R_i(z)[/latex] and [latex]W_i(z)[/latex] denote read and write operations on a data element [latex]z[/latex] by a transaction [latex]T_i[/latex], respectively. Consider the schedule [latex]S[/latex] with four transactions.

S: [latex]R_4(x)R_2(x)R_3(x)R_1(y)W_1(y)W_2 (x)W_3 (y)R_4(y)[/latex]

Which one of the following serial schedules is conflict equivalent to [latex]S[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Conflicting pairs in S:
- [latex]R_4(x)[/latex] before [latex]W_2(x)[/latex]: T4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T2
- [latex]R_3(x)[/latex] before [latex]W_2(x)[/latex]: T3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T2
- [latex]R_1(y)/W_1(y)[/latex] before [latex]W_3(y)[/latex]: T1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T3
- [latex]W_1(y)[/latex] before [latex]R_4(y)[/latex]: T1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T4
- [latex]W_3(y)[/latex] before [latex]R_4(y)[/latex]: T3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T4

Topological order: T1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T2.

Answer: [latex]T_1\rightarrow T_3\rightarrow T_4\rightarrow T_2[/latex]

questions.text:
Consider a relation [latex]R( A, B, C, D, E )[/latex] with the following three functional dependencies.
[latex]AB \rightarrow C;BC \rightarrow D; C \rightarrow E;[/latex]
The number of superkeys in the relation [latex]R[/latex] is .
questions.solution:
A and B never appear on the right side of any FD, so every key must contain A and B.
[latex]AB^+=AB\rightarrow ABC\rightarrow ABCD\rightarrow ABCDE[/latex], so AB is the only candidate key.

Superkeys = AB plus any subset of {C, D, E}: [latex]2^3=8[/latex].

Answer: 8

questions.text:
Consider the following three relations in a relational database.
[latex]Employee(eId, Name), Brand (bId, bName), Own(eId ,bId)[/latex]
Which of the following relational algebra expressions return the set of [latex]eIds[/latex] who own all the brands?
questions.solution:
"Owns all brands" is relational division by the set of all brands.

- Option 1: [latex]\Pi_{eId,bId}(Own)\div\Pi_{bId}(Brand)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] exactly division [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 2: [latex]\Pi_{eId}(Own)\times\Pi_{bId}(Brand)[/latex] lists every (employee, brand) pair; subtracting Own leaves the pairs an employee does not own. Removing those employees leaves those who own every brand [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (this is the expansion of division).
- Option 3 divides by [latex]\Pi_{bId}(Own)[/latex] (brands owned by someone); a brand owned by nobody would be ignored [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.
- Option 4 divides a full cross product, which returns every employee [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

questions.text: In a relational data model, which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Relation R(A, B): the only possible non-trivial FDs are [latex]A\rightarrow B[/latex] or [latex]B\rightarrow A[/latex]. In each case the left side is a key, so R is always in BCNF [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- All attributes prime guarantees 3NF, not BCNF (e.g. [latex]AB\rightarrow C,\ C\rightarrow B[/latex]) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- A relation can have no non-prime attribute (e.g. all attributes form the key) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- BCNF decomposition does not always preserve FDs [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF.
If all attributes of a relation are prime attributes, then the relation is in BCNF.
Every relation has at least one non-prime attribute.
